title: Supervised versus unsupervised
story:
The usual framing is that one kind has labels and the other does not, which is true and makes it sound like a difference of convenience. The difference that matters is whether there is anything you can be wrong about.

With a target, error is defined. The learned rule either agrees with the target on a given input or it does not, the guarantee bounds the probability of disagreement beyond a stated amount, and the whole apparatus of held-out estimation works because you can check the answer. That is what made the previous lesson's framework statable at all: the existence of a target concept to disagree with.

Without one, none of that structure exists, and it is important not to reach for its vocabulary anyway. Take the best-known example. MacQueen coined the term k-means in 1967, describing methods for classification and analysis of multivariate observations, and the procedure partitions the data to minimise a within-group criterion. Two things about it are decisions rather than discoveries: the number of groups is supplied, not found, and the criterion is chosen by the analyst. Run it and you will get groups. You will always get groups. Ask whether they are the right groups and there is no fact of the matter to appeal to, because nothing in the data says how many there should be or what makes a good one.

This is not a criticism of the method, and the honest position is not that unsupervised work is unscientific. It is that the objective is the assumption, made explicit. Choosing to minimise within-group spread is a claim that the structure you care about is compact and roughly spherical in the space you happen to be using. That claim may be right. It is not tested by the algorithm that assumes it.

So there are only two defensible ways to evaluate the second kind. Against the criterion you chose, which is circular but at least legible — you can say the partition is good by the standard used to produce it. Or against something downstream: the segments led to a campaign that performed better, the reduced representation made a supervised model score higher, the grouping matched a judgement somebody trusted. That second route converts the problem back into the first, which is usually the right move when a decision depends on it.

problem.name: The presence of a target
problem.shape: You have data and a goal, and the goal either names an answer for each row or it does not.
tell: there is a column you would act on if you could predict it
the number of groups is a parameter somebody chose
the method will produce output regardless of whether structure exists
an evaluation is being described as accuracy when no target exists
problem.move: Decide first whether an error is definable. If it is, hold out data and estimate it. If it is not, state the objective you are choosing and what it assumes about the shape of the structure, then evaluate against something downstream that does have an answer.
problem.invariant: A held-out estimate requires a quantity that can be right or wrong. Where no target exists, the objective supplies the standard, and the standard is therefore an assumption rather than a measurement.
problem.breaks: The distinction is about the goal, not the data, and the same table supports both — so a dataset with labels can still be approached without them, and a clustering can become supervised the moment somebody decides one of its outputs is the thing to predict. What changes is what would count as being wrong.

cost.time: converting an unsupervised question into a downstream supervised one costs an experiment, which is the price of getting an answer that can be checked
cost.beats: reporting an internal criterion as though it were a validation score, which reads as evidence and is a restatement of the objective

worked.problem: How would you know whether a clustering is any good?
worked.reasoning:
By being clear that the question as asked has no answer, and then converting it into one that does.

The reason is structural. With a target, good means close to the target, and a held-out estimate measures that. Without one, there is nothing to be close to. The algorithm will partition the data whatever the data looks like — supply the number of groups and it supplies the groups, on structure or on noise alike.

That leaves three things I can actually do, in increasing order of usefulness.

The weakest is to evaluate against the criterion that produced the partition. Within-group spread is low, so the clustering is good by the standard used to make it. This is circular, and it is worth saying so rather than presenting it as validation. It has one legitimate use: comparing runs that share the objective, such as choosing among initialisations.

Better is to check stability. Resample or perturb the data, cluster again, and see whether the same structure reappears. A partition that changes completely under resampling is describing the sample rather than the population. This does not tell you the clustering is right, but it can tell you it is arbitrary, which is often the finding that matters.

Best is to evaluate downstream, against something that does have an answer. The segments were used to target an intervention and the intervention performed measurably better. The reduced representation improved a supervised model's held-out score. The grouping was shown to someone whose judgement is the actual standard and they recognised it. Each converts the question back into one with a target, which is the only setting where good is defined.

I would also state the assumption out loud, because it is usually invisible. Minimising within-group spread assumes the structure of interest is compact and roughly spherical in whatever space the features happen to define — and since that space came from choices about scaling and encoding, the clustering is partly a consequence of the preprocessing rather than of the data.

problem.practice: Take a clustering you trust and run it again on a resample of the same data. Compare the two partitions. Then write down, in one sentence, what shape of structure your objective assumed — and whether the scaling choices you made earlier were what put that shape into the space.

beats.broke: Two activities share one heading — recovering a rule that maps inputs to a known answer, and finding structure where no answer exists — and they differ in whether there is anything to be wrong about.
beats.fix: Ask what would count as an error before choosing a method. With a target, error is measurable and a held-out estimate means something; without one, the objective you chose is the only standard there is.
beats.cost: In the second case the objective is the assumption, so the result cannot be validated in the sense the first case allows — only checked against the criterion that produced it, or against what it is later used for.

interview.q: How would you know whether a clustering is any good?
interview.trap: Reaching for an internal criterion and reporting it as though it were a validation score. Low within-group spread says the partition is good by the standard used to create it, which is a restatement of the objective rather than evidence for it.
interview.answer:

With a target, good means close to the target and a held-out estimate measures it. Without one there is nothing to be close to, and the algorithm will partition the data regardless of what the data looks like — supply the number of groups and it supplies them, on structure and on noise alike.

Best is downstream evaluation against something that does have an answer — the segments drove an intervention that measurably performed better, the representation improved a supervised model's held-out score, or the grouping was recognised by someone whose judgement is the real standard. Each converts the question back into one with a target, which is the only setting where good is defined.

takeaway: The distinction is not labels but whether an error is definable — and since a clustering algorithm returns groups on noise as readily as on structure, the objective you chose is an assumption about shape rather than a measurement of it.
